instructions: Answer all four questions. Where a diagram is asked for, draw it on paper, photograph it and upload it with the 🖼 button. Use the √x button for equations.

questions.question: Define a deadlock. State the four Coffman conditions and explain, with one example each, how breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.
questions.guidance: About 200 words. A table of the four conditions is acceptable.
questions.modelAnswer: Definition (2). Four conditions named — mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait (2). One prevention example per condition (4).

questions.question: Draw a resource-allocation graph for three processes and three resource types that is deadlocked, and show how the graph changes once the deadlock is broken.
questions.guidance: Draw it on paper and upload a clear photograph. Label every node and edge.
questions.modelAnswer: Correct graph with a cycle (3). Correct explanation of the cycle (1). Correct post-break graph (2). Unlabelled diagrams: half marks.

questions.question: A system has 5 processes and 3 resource types. Apply the Banker's algorithm to decide whether the state below is safe, and write out the safe sequence if one exists. Show every step.
questions.guidance: Show the Need matrix and the Work vector at each step. Use the equation editor for the matrices if you prefer.
questions.modelAnswer: Need matrix computed correctly (3). Each correct step of the safety check (5). Correct conclusion and safe sequence (2).

questions.question: Compare deadlock prevention, avoidance and detection-and-recovery on cost, resource utilisation and practicality. Which does a general-purpose operating system actually use, and why?
questions.guidance: A comparison table followed by a short paragraph works well here.
questions.modelAnswer: Three strategies compared on all three axes (4). Correct observation that most OSs ignore deadlock — the ostrich algorithm — with justification (2).
